title: Event-Driven Systems and Stream Processing
html:
Event-Driven Systems and Stream Processing

Chapter 11 introduced local Catalog projections so that consumers could serve reads without calling Catalog for every request. Maintaining those projections requires durable event delivery, an explicit rule for applying repeated or out-of-order events, and a recovery procedure when consumers fall behind.

An event records a completed fact, such as “order 4471 was confirmed.” The publishing service can commit its transaction without waiting for each consumer to update a projection, send an email, or record an analytic result. Those consumers run independently and may process the event later, more than once, or after a restart. At Baodium, this separation reduced synchronous dependencies while introducing new questions about delivery, completion, and recovery.

The Notification Pipeline

Baodium’s order-confirmation emails are a good example of both the benefit and the cost. In the original design, Order Service sent the email as part of the checkout request: it saved the order, called the email provider, and returned the confirmation page only after the provider replied.

That arrangement made checkout depend on the email provider. When the provider was slow, every checkout was slow by the same amount. When the provider returned an error, the checkout request failed even though the order had already been saved, and a customer who tried again could create a second order. An optional notification was affecting a required operation, which is the kind of coupling events are meant to remove.

The team therefore took the email out of the checkout request. The pipeline now has four steps:

  1. Order Service saves the order and an outbox record in a single database transaction.

  2. A relay process reads new outbox records and publishes them to Kafka, a durable message log.

  3. Notification Service reads each event from Kafka and records a task to send an email.

  4. Sender workers submit those tasks to the email provider.

Checkout now completes after step 1, so the email provider can no longer slow down or fail a purchase. Steps 2 through 4 run afterward in other processes. The rest of the chapter is about making that later work reliable, starting with the design of step 1.

The Transactional Outbox

Why does step 1 write an outbox record instead of publishing to Kafka directly? To see the reason, consider what happens when a customer confirms an order. The application has to do two things: save the order in Order Service’s database, and publish an OrderConfirmed event to Kafka so that other services can react to it.

Order Service’s database and Kafka each acknowledge their own writes. A successful database commit tells us nothing about whether Kafka received the event. Suppose the order is saved and the process crashes before publication. The order exists, but Notification Service never learns to send the email. Publishing first creates the opposite risk: consumers could act on an order whose database transaction later rolls back.

This is a common distributed-systems problem. Two services can be healthy and still disagree about what happened because the operation crossed a boundary where neither controls the other’s commit. The design needs a durable record of work that remains to be done after the first commit.

The transactional outbox solves this by removing Kafka from the transaction. Instead of publishing directly, Order Service writes the event as a row in an ordinary database table, the outbox, in the same transaction that saves the order. Because both rows are in one database, the database can guarantee that both are saved or neither is. A separate relay reads committed outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, retrying after inconclusive submissions. The database transaction prevents an acknowledged business change from omitting its outbox obligation; eventual publication also depends on retaining those records, durable storage, and a functioning relay and broker. Publication can therefore be delayed and must be monitored and repaired.

The name comes from the tray on an office desk. A clerk finishes a letter and places it in the outbox as part of the same task, and the mail room collects it later. The clerk does not have to stop and deliver the letter personally, and the letter is not lost if the clerk leaves for the day.

The Promotion Incident

The outbox made the pipeline safe to build, but it did not make the pipeline fast. Forty minutes into a large promotion, customers began reporting that their confirmation emails had not arrived. The on-call engineer proposed doubling the number of Kafka consumers in Notification Service, on the reasonable assumption that Notification Service was falling behind on reading events.

The consumer-lag graph did not support that assumption. Consumer lag measures how far a consumer is behind the newest events in Kafka, and it was close to zero, which meant Notification Service was reading events almost as soon as they were published.

The delay was in the sender stage. Notification Service was creating email tasks at about 12,000 per minute, but the senders were getting only about 10,000 per minute accepted by the provider. The difference, 2,000 tasks per minute, was accumulating in Notification Service’s database, which the lag graph does not measure. More consumers could only have created tasks faster; they could not have sent more email.

The incident raised two questions that the rest of this chapter answers: how do we find the stage that is behind, and what does each stage’s report of success mean? We begin with the second question, because it determines how we answer the first.

Completion Semantics

When a dashboard says that an event was processed, what exactly has finished? For Notification Service, the answer was task creation. For each event, the consumer read the event from Kafka, wrote a task to the database, and incremented its “processed” counter. At that point, no email had been sent; the task was waiting for a sender. During the promotion, the counter showed every event processed while hundreds of thousands of emails remained unsent.

The counter was accurate for the stage it measured, but each stage completes a distinct piece of work, and the first stage’s success says nothing about the later ones. Table \(\ref{tab:notification-boundaries}\) shows what each stage guarantees and what work remains after it.

For the rest of this chapter, a notification counts as submitted when the provider’s acceptance is recorded against its task. Acceptance does not mean the email reached an inbox; delivery reports and bounces measure that separately.

Once we define completion this way, the measurement has to include unfinished work. A latency chart built from successful submissions contains only the tasks that were sent, so it understates how long customers have waited while a backlog is growing. Baodium therefore reports the number of overdue unfinished tasks alongside completion times. Tasks that are suppressed, canceled, or permanently failed receive their own outcomes, because removing a task from the queue is not the same as sending it.

Backlog Dynamics

With completion defined, we can ask how quickly a backlog grows and how long it takes to clear. Backlog increases when new tasks arrive faster than workers complete them and decreases when completion rate exceeds arrival rate. The net rate determines whether waiting work is accumulating or being processed during recovery.

During the promotion, tasks arrived at 12,000 per minute and completed at 10,000 per minute, so the backlog grew by 2,000 every minute. After three hours, about 360,000 tasks were waiting. If new orders had stopped altogether, the senders could have cleared that backlog in 36 minutes.

New orders do not stop during a promotion, however. Suppose the team raises sender throughput to 14,000 per minute while tasks continue to arrive at 12,000. The first 12,000 completions each minute only keep pace with new arrivals, so only the remaining 2,000 reduce the backlog. At that rate, clearing 360,000 tasks takes 180 minutes. At a net recovery rate of 2,000 tasks per minute, those 360,000 tasks require three hours to clear while new work continues arriving.

In general, for a backlog \(B\), an arrival rate \(\lambda\), and a completion rate \(\mu\), the time to drain is

\[T_{\mathrm{drain}} = \frac{B}{\mu-\lambda}, \qquad \mu>\lambda.\]

The denominator is the gap between the drain and the tap. If the completion rate only matches the arrival rate, the backlog never shrinks, and if it exceeds the arrival rate by a small margin, the backlog shrinks slowly. In practice, recovery is slower than the formula suggests, because tasks that fail during recovery are retried and add to the arrivals.

Backlog Size and Backlog Age

Backlog depth measures unfinished work. To determine how long customers have been waiting, Baodium also records the age of its oldest unfinished task. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch12-lag}\) shows how far the two measures can diverge.

If senders handle tasks strictly in the order they were created, the oldest unfinished task after three hours is about thirty minutes old, because by then the senders have completed every task created in the first two and a half hours. Parallel senders, retries, and priorities make that relationship less predictable, so the dashboard reads the age directly from the timestamps of unfinished tasks.

The dashboard also separates first attempts from retries, because the two point to separate problems. If every task is late, the senders lack capacity. If most tasks finish on time while a small group keeps failing, adding capacity will not help, and the failing tasks need to be investigated.

Queues, Logs, and Retention

So far we have treated Kafka as a pipe between Order Service and Notification Service. To understand what a consumer can recover after a failure, we need to look at what Kafka keeps, and for how long. Messaging systems follow one of two designs, which Figure \(\ref{fig:ch12-queue-log}\) contrasts.

A queue works like a to-do list shared by a group of workers. Each item goes to one worker, and once that worker confirms it has finished, the item is crossed off and removed.

A log works like a newspaper archive. Every record is added to the end and kept for a set period. Each reader keeps track of its own place, so many readers can read the same records independently, and any reader can go back and reread older ones.

The difference determines what we can build later. Suppose that, six months after launch, Baodium adds an analytics service that counts orders by region. With a log, the new service can read the same order events that Notification Service reads, going back as far as the log retains them, without any change to Order Service. With a queue, those events were removed as soon as Notification Service handled them, so the new service sees only orders placed after it starts.

Kafka uses the log design. Events are grouped into topics, such as order-events, and each group of consumers keeps its own place in each topic. Notification Service and the analytics service can therefore read the same events without affecting each other.

Retention and Compaction

A log cannot keep everything forever, so Kafka deletes old records according to a retention setting, usually a time limit or a size limit. Deletion happens whether or not every consumer has read the records, so a consumer that is down for longer than the retention period loses the events it missed.

Kafka also offers compaction. Over time, compaction removes older records for a key while retaining its most recently published value, subject to tombstone and retention settings. A product-state topic keyed by product identifier can therefore support rebuilding a local catalog projection from the latest retained values. That projection is current only as far as Catalog has published updates and the consumer has applied them. Historical product prices require separate records, because compaction may remove previous values.

Listing \(\ref{lst:ch12-topics}\) creates one topic of each kind: order events kept for fourteen days, and product state compacted to the latest record per product. We return to the replication settings when we discuss publication.

[
  caption={Creating a retained event topic and a compacted state topic.},
  label={lst:ch12-topics}]
# Order events: every record kept for 14 days
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --create \
  --topic order-events --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 \
  --config retention.ms=1209600000 \
  --config min.insync.replicas=2

# Product state: latest record for each product key, kept indefinitely
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --create \
  --topic product-state --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 \
  --config cleanup.policy=compact \
  --config min.insync.replicas=2

Retention Sizing

How long should retention be? It has to be longer than the slowest recovery we expect. Suppose a consumer fails on Monday morning, the team needs two days to diagnose and fix it, and the repaired consumer then needs a day to process the events it missed. With two-day retention, Kafka deletes Monday’s events on Wednesday morning, while the consumer is catching up, and those events cannot be recovered from Kafka.

The retention period therefore needs to cover four intervals: detecting the failure, fixing it, catching up, and any investigation that follows. Once events have been deleted, recovery needs another source, such as an archive or a snapshot of the owning service’s data.

Partitions, Offsets, and Consumer Groups

If each topic were a single log, only one consumer could read it in order, and throughput is limited to what one process can handle. Kafka avoids this limit by dividing each topic into partitions, independent logs that can be read in parallel. Three terms describe how consumers read them:

Offset.

Every record in a partition has a position number called its offset. Offsets start at zero and increase by one for each new record.

Committed offset.

Each consumer saves the offset it has reached, like a bookmark, so that it can resume from the same place after a restart.

Consumer group.

Consumers that share the work of reading a topic form a group, and the group divides the partitions among its members.

Figure \(\ref{fig:ch12-partitions}\) shows a group dividing a topic’s partitions.

Within a group, each partition is read by exactly one consumer at a time, although one consumer can read several partitions. With twelve partitions and four consumers, each consumer reads three; with twelve consumers, each reads one. A thirteenth consumer has no partition to read. As a result, the partition count is the upper limit on parallelism within a group, and it is the first number to check when someone proposes adding consumers.

Message Keys and Ordering

Partitions give us parallelism, but they also change the ordering guarantee. Kafka keeps records in order within a partition, but not across partitions. If an order’s OrderShipped event went to partition 3 and its OrderConfirmed event went to partition 7, a consumer could process the shipment before the confirmation.

Producers prevent this by giving each record a key. Records with the same key always go to the same partition, so their relative order is preserved. Baodium uses order_id as the key for order events, which means all events for one order land in one partition and are read in the order they were written.

Kafka can preserve only the order in which records arrive, however. If the relay publishes an order’s events in the wrong order, Kafka stores them in the wrong order. We will see how the relay avoids this when we look at publication.

Keys have two further consequences. First, a single busy key cannot be spread across consumers: if one exceptionally large merchant produces a flood of events under one key, those events all go to one partition and one consumer, and adding consumers does not speed them up. Second, changing the number of partitions reshuffles keys. Kafka chooses a partition from a hash of the key and the partition count, so after partitions are added, new events for an order can go to a new partition while its older events wait in the old one. Teams that need more partitions therefore usually create a new topic and migrate consumers to it in a controlled way.

Out-of-Order Delivery

Even with keys, a consumer can sometimes receive events out of order, for example after a producer retries a failed send. Each consumer needs a rule for this situation, and the right rule depends on what the event contains.

Suppose a Catalog copy receives product version 12 before version 11. If each event contains the complete product, version 12 is all the consumer needs, so it applies version 12 and discards version 11 when it arrives. If each event describes only a change, such as “price reduced by $5,” applying version 12 without version 11 produces the wrong price, so the consumer must detect the gap and fetch the missing version first. The event contract should therefore state which kind of event it is, because the two kinds require opposite handling.

Event Publication

With partitions and keys in place, we can return to step 2 of the pipeline and look at how the relay transfers events from the outbox into Kafka. Listing \(\ref{lst:ch12-envelope}\) shows one published event, and each of its fields has a specific purpose:

message_id

identifies this particular event, so a consumer can recognize it if it arrives twice.

event_type and schema_version

tell the consumer how to interpret the payload.

occurred_at

records when the business action happened.

order_version

lets a consumer detect events for the same order that arrive out of order.

[
  caption={An order event as published to Kafka.},
  label={lst:ch12-envelope}]
{
  "message_id": "3f0c9a6e-2c41-4f7b-9d8e-5b1a7c2e4f10",
  "event_type": "OrderConfirmed",
  "schema_version": 2,
  "occurred_at": "2026-03-14T10:00:03.214Z",
  "order_id": "ord_4471",
  "order_version": 3,
  "payload": {
    "customer_ref": "cus_88213",
    "total_minor_units": 12950,
    "currency": "USD"
  }
}

The Relay Loop

Listing \(\ref{lst:ch12-outbox}\) shows the outbox table and the query the relay uses to claim work. The relay repeats the same four steps:

  1. Claim a batch of the oldest unpublished outbox rows.

  2. Publish each row to Kafka, using the order identifier as the key.

  3. Wait until Kafka confirms it has stored every record.

  4. Mark the batch as published and commit.

[
  language=SQL,
  caption={The outbox table and the relay's claim query.},
  label={lst:ch12-outbox}]
CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  message_id    UUID NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  aggregate_key TEXT NOT NULL,      -- order_id, used as the Kafka key
  event_type    TEXT NOT NULL,
  payload       JSONB NOT NULL,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at  TIMESTAMPTZ
);

CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON outbox (id)
  WHERE published_at IS NULL;

-- Relay: claim the oldest unpublished events in this relay's shard
SELECT id, message_id, aggregate_key, event_type, payload
FROM outbox
WHERE published_at IS NULL
  AND (hashtext(aggregate_key) & 2147483647) % 4 = :shard
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 500
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Consider what happens if the relay crashes between steps 3 and 4. Kafka has stored the events, but the outbox shows them as unpublished, because the relay stopped before recording its success. When the relay restarts, it claims the same rows and publishes them again, so Kafka now holds two copies of each event in that batch.

Marking an outbox row as published before Kafka acknowledges it would create a different failure: a relay crash could permanently omit the event. The relay therefore permits repeated publication after an uncertain acknowledgement. Each event includes a message_id that consumers use to recognize repeated delivery without repeating the business effect.

Relay Sharding

A single relay may not keep up with a busy outbox, so Baodium runs several. The clause FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets each relay claim rows that no other relay is holding, without waiting for locks.

Running several relays creates an ordering problem, however. Relay A might claim an order’s OrderConfirmed event while relay B claims the same order’s OrderShipped event in a separate batch. If relay A is briefly delayed, relay B publishes first, and Kafka stores the shipment ahead of the confirmation. The key maps both events to the same partition, but Kafka preserves the order of publication; it cannot correct an earlier relay reordering.

Baodium assigns each outbox shard to one active relay and fences its previous owner before transferring that assignment. Hashing the order identifier ensures that events for one order use the same shard. The relay publishes those events in the order of their committed business versions. That requires an additional guarantee from Order Service: transitions for one order acquire the same row lock, and each transaction inserts its outbox row only after obtaining that lock. A subsequent transition cannot allocate its outbox identifier until the preceding transaction commits. Without that serialization rule, BIGSERIAL allocation order would not prove business order, because PostgreSQL sequences advance independently of commit order. The relay must also avoid skipping an unpublished earlier version when a later version is available; the consumer checks order_version and pauses or reconciles a gap rather than applying an event out of order.

An alternative is a change-data-capture tool such as Debezium, which reads the database’s own change log and publishes outbox rows in the order they were committed. That removes the polling query and the sharding logic, at the cost of another system to deploy, monitor, and upgrade.

Producer Acknowledgments and Durability

Step 3 of the relay loop waits for Kafka to confirm each record, but what does that confirmation guarantee? The answer depends on the producer settings in Listing \(\ref{lst:ch12-producer}\).

[
  caption={Producer settings for the outbox relay.},
  label={lst:ch12-producer}]
acks=all
enable.idempotence=true
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5
delivery.timeout.ms=120000

Kafka stores each partition on several servers, called brokers, so that the failure of one server does not lose data. A confirmation is only as durable as the number of copies that exist when it is sent, and two settings control that:

acks=all

makes Kafka confirm a record only after every up-to-date copy has stored it. Combined with the topic setting min.insync.replicas=2 from Listing \(\ref{lst:ch12-topics}\), Kafka refuses writes unless at least two copies can be made. With three copies of each partition, a confirmed event survives the loss of any one broker.

enable.idempotence=true

lets Kafka discard duplicates caused by the relay’s own network retries. Each batch includes a sequence number, and Kafka ignores a batch it has already stored.

Producer idempotence has a narrow scope, though: it recognizes retries only within one producer session. When the relay crashes and restarts, it begins a new session, and Kafka cannot tell that the restarted relay’s records are repeats. Those duplicates are handled by the message_id and the consumer-side deduplication we cover next.

Delivery Semantics

We now turn to step 3 of the pipeline, where Notification Service reads events. To understand what can go wrong there, we need to look at how a consumer keeps track of its progress.

Every consumer tracks two numbers. Its position is the next record Kafka will hand it, and its committed offset is the bookmark it has saved, the point from which it resumes after a restart. By convention, the bookmark points at the next record to read, so after finishing the record at offset 42, the consumer commits 43.

The gap between reading a record and committing the bookmark is where failures cause trouble. Suppose the consumer reads offset 42, creates the email task, and crashes before it commits 43. When it restarts, its bookmark is 42, so it reads offset 42 again and processes the same event a second time.

At-Most-Once and At-Least-Once

The point at which a consumer commits decides what a crash can do:

Commit after the work.

A crash can make the consumer repeat a record, but it can never lose one. This is at-least-once delivery.

Commit before the work.

A crash can make the consumer lose a record, but it can never repeat one. This is at-most-once delivery.

Baodium uses at-least-once delivery for business events because losing an accepted order notification would be worse than receiving the same event again. If the consumer completes its database transaction but stops before committing its offset, Kafka can return that event when the consumer restarts. The second delivery must not create a second business effect.

Every consumer therefore has to be idempotent, which means that processing the same record twice has the same effect as processing it once. The consumer also needs a clear point at which a record’s work is durably finished, because that is the earliest moment it may commit. For Notification Service, that point is when the email task exists in the database; from then on, the obligation to send the email survives anything that happens to the consumer.

Consumer Configuration

By default, Kafka clients commit the bookmark automatically every few seconds, whether or not the application has finished its work. An automatic commit can therefore advance past a record whose task was never created, which turns at-least-once delivery into at-most-once without any warning. Listing \(\ref{lst:ch12-consumer}\) shows the settings Baodium uses instead, and the list that follows explains each one.

[
  caption={Consumer settings for Notification Service's task creator.},
  label={lst:ch12-consumer}]
group.id=notification-task-creator
enable.auto.commit=false
auto.offset.reset=earliest
isolation.level=read_committed
max.poll.records=200
max.poll.interval.ms=300000
partition.assignment.strategy=\
  org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor
group.instance.id=notification-task-creator-3
enable.auto.commit=false

The application commits only after the task exists.

auto.offset.reset=earliest

A group with no saved bookmark starts from the oldest retained event rather than the newest. A new group may process some events twice, but it never skips any.

isolation.level=read_committed

The consumer ignores records from producer transactions that were aborted.

max.poll.records, max.poll.interval.ms

These form an agreement with Kafka: the consumer will finish up to 200 records and ask for more within five minutes. A consumer that misses that deadline is assumed to have failed, and its partitions are reassigned.

partition.assignment.strategy, group.instance.id

These reduce the disruption when partitions are reassigned, as we discuss under consumer rebalancing.

Idempotent Consumers

Because Kafka can redeliver a record after a consumer restart, Notification Service creates tasks using the event’s message_id as a deduplication key. In the same transaction that creates a task, the consumer records that identifier in a table with a uniqueness constraint. When a repeated event arrives, its identifier is already recorded, so no second task is created. Listing \(\ref{lst:ch12-task}\) shows the consumer’s logic.

def process_order_event(record, db, consumer):
    event = decode_and_validate(record.value)

    with db.transaction() as tx:
        first_delivery = tx.claim_event(
            consumer="notification-task-creator",
            message_id=event.message_id,
        )

        if first_delivery:
            tx.create_notification_task(
                event_id=event.message_id,
                order_id=event.order_id,
                notification_type="order_confirmation",
                state="PENDING",
            )

    consumer.commit_next_offset(
        topic=record.topic,
        partition=record.partition,
        offset=record.offset + 1,
    )

It might seem sufficient to check whether the identifier exists and insert it if it does not, but that approach fails when two copies of the same event are processed at the same moment. Both threads check, both find nothing, and both insert, so two tasks are created. Each thread reasoned correctly about a table that changed between its check and its insert, which is the check-then-act problem from Chapter 9. The “recorded once” rule therefore has to be enforced by the database.

Listing \(\ref{lst:ch12-claim}\) shows how to do that in PostgreSQL. The statement INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING performs the check and the insert as one atomic operation. When two copies race, exactly one insert succeeds and only that one returns a row, which is how claim_event knows it is handling the first delivery.

[
  language=SQL,
  caption={Claiming an event and enforcing one confirmation per order.},
  label={lst:ch12-claim}]
CREATE TABLE processed_events (
  consumer     TEXT NOT NULL,
  message_id   UUID NOT NULL,
  processed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (consumer, message_id)
);

-- claim_event: returns a row only for the first delivery
INSERT INTO processed_events (consumer, message_id)
VALUES ('notification-task-creator', :message_id)
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
RETURNING message_id;

-- Business rule: at most one confirmation task per order
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_confirmation_per_order
  ON notification_tasks (order_id)
  WHERE notification_type = 'order_confirmation';

The unique index at the end of the listing adds a second safeguard at the business level, by allowing at most one confirmation task per order. Even if a producer bug gave the same confirmation two identifiers, the customer could not receive two confirmation emails.

Three further rules keep the scheme sound. First, the producer assigns the message_id once, when it writes the outbox row, and every publication retry reuses it; a hash of the payload is not a substitute, because two genuine events can have identical contents. Second, claims must be kept for as long as an event can be redelivered or replayed, since a repeated event whose claim has been deleted looks new. Third, a consumer that processes several records at once may commit only up to the first unfinished record. If offset 42 finishes while offset 41 is in progress, committing 43 and then crashing skips offset 41.

External Side Effects

Idempotent task creation handles step 3, but step 4 is harder. Creating a task is a write to Baodium’s own database, where a uniqueness constraint can reject a duplicate. Sending an email is a call to another company’s system, and no constraint in Baodium’s database can reach it.

Consider what happens when a sender submits an email and the network drops the provider’s reply. The provider has accepted the email and will deliver it, but the sender sees only a timeout, which looks the same as a failed submission. If the sender retries, the customer may receive two emails; if it does not, a submission that did fail is never sent. The sender cannot make the right choice, because it does not know whether the provider received the first attempt.

Two provider features supply that missing information. An idempotency key lets the sender attach an identifier to each submission, so that the provider can recognize a retry and ignore it. A status lookup lets the sender ask whether a submission with a given identifier arrived. Chapter 3 dealt with the same problem for payments, where a duplicate means charging a customer twice. A duplicate email is much less serious, but the notification contract should state whether duplicates are acceptable. If the provider offers neither feature, the team has to decide between risking duplicates and risking missing emails, and that decision should be recorded in the design rather than left to the default behavior of a retry library.

Task States and Leases

Because several sender processes share the task table, and any of them can crash halfway through a submission, each task needs an explicit state. Baodium uses six:

PENDING

The task is waiting for its first attempt.

SENDING

A sender has claimed the task and is submitting it.

ACCEPTED

The provider has accepted the email.

RETRY_SCHEDULED

The provider rejected the submission temporarily, and the task will be retried later.

UNCERTAIN

A sender crashed during submission, and it is unknown whether the provider received the email.

FAILED

The task has used up its attempts or its time.

Listing \(\ref{lst:ch12-lease}\) shows how a sender claims a batch of tasks.

[
  language=SQL,
  caption={A sender claiming due tasks with a lease.},
  label={lst:ch12-lease}]
UPDATE notification_tasks
SET state = 'SENDING',
    lease_expires_at = now() + interval '2 minutes',
    attempt = attempt + 1
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM notification_tasks
  WHERE state IN ('PENDING', 'RETRY_SCHEDULED')
    AND next_attempt_at <= now()
  ORDER BY next_attempt_at
  LIMIT 100
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
RETURNING id, order_id, attempt;

As with the relay, SKIP LOCKED lets many senders claim separate tasks without waiting for one another. The lease deals with senders that crash. A claimed task belongs to its sender for two minutes, and if the sender crashes, the lease expires and a recovery job finds the task in the SENDING state.

The recovery job cannot return the task to PENDING, because the crashed sender may have reached the provider before it stopped, and resending could produce a duplicate. Instead, the task becomes UNCERTAIN. Because every sender uses the task’s identifier as the provider’s idempotency key, recovery can ask the provider whether that submission arrived and resubmit only if the provider has no record of it.

Exponential Backoff and Jitter

When the provider rejects a submission temporarily, the task becomes RETRY_SCHEDULED, and the sender has to choose when to try again. A fixed delay seems natural, but it creates a problem. If a provider outage makes ten thousand tasks fail within the same minute, a fixed five-minute delay schedules all ten thousand retries for the same minute five minutes later, and the provider, which has only recently recovered, receives a burst much larger than its normal traffic.

Baodium therefore uses exponential backoff with full jitter. The maximum delay doubles with each attempt, and the actual delay is a random value between zero and that maximum:

\[\text{delay} = \mathrm{random}\bigl(0,\ \min(\mathit{cap},\ \mathit{base} \times 2^{\mathit{attempt}})\bigr).\]

With a base of 10 seconds and a cap of 15 minutes, a task on its fifth attempt waits a random interval of up to 320 seconds. The doubling gives a struggling provider more time to recover with each attempt, and the randomness spreads the retries across that interval so that they arrive gradually rather than all at once. After a maximum number of attempts or a maximum age, the task becomes FAILED with a recorded reason, so it is counted as a failed notification instead of disappearing from the backlog.

Exactly-Once Semantics

You will often hear that Kafka provides exactly-once processing, so we need to be precise about what that means. Kafka transactions can save a consumer’s bookmark and its output to Kafka in one atomic step, which gives exactly-once processing for a stage that reads from Kafka and writes only back to Kafka. Those transactions cannot include a PostgreSQL write or a call to an email provider.

An exactly-once claim is therefore meaningful only when it names the output it covers. Notification Service guarantees exactly one task per event, because it combines at-least-once delivery with idempotent task creation. It guarantees exactly one email only to the extent that the provider honors its idempotency key.

::: decision

**Which stage do you scale?**

During the promotion, Notification Service is creating about 12,000 delivery tasks per minute while senders record roughly 10,000 provider acceptances per minute. Kafka consumer lag is low. The backlog of unfinished tasks has been growing for three hours, and the oldest unfinished task is now about thirty minutes old.

**Add Kafka consumers, since the event stream is where the work arrives.**

**Add senders, or raise the provider’s rate allowance.**

**Defer the promotion’s optional marketing emails until the backlog drains.**

—

Tasks are created at 12,000 per minute and completed at 10,000, so the backlog grows by 2,000 per minute regardless of consumer capacity.

A adds capacity before the backlog. The consumers already keep up, so adding more of them creates tasks no faster and sends no more email.

B targets the stage where work accumulates, but it helps only if sender capacity is the binding limit. If the provider’s rate allowance is the limit, more senders achieve nothing and may trigger rate-limit rejections that look like a new failure. Determine which limit applies before adding senders.

C reduces the arrival rate. When completion cannot be raised quickly, reducing arrivals is the remaining option, and deferring optional marketing emails frees capacity for confirmations without dropping any promised notification. It also raises a question to settle in advance: should a confirmation that is hours late be sent at all?

:::

Backlog Diagnosis

We can now return to the first question from the incident: how do we find the stage that is behind? Each stage of the pipeline produces its own symptom, and Table \(\ref{tab:event-observability}\) maps each symptom to the stage it points to.

Consumer lag is the gap between the newest offset in a partition and the group’s committed offset. It measures progress through the retained log, without establishing whether the downstream notification or business task has finished. Low lag shows that the consumer has reached its own finishing point, which for Notification Service is task creation, but it says nothing about the stages after it.

For that reason, the sender stage has its own measurements: task arrivals, provider acceptances, retries, uncertain tasks, failures, and the age of the oldest unfinished task. Kafka measurements are shown per partition, so that a single overloaded partition does not disappear into an average.

Listing \(\ref{lst:ch12-lag}\) shows the two checks an engineer runs during an incident. For each partition, the Kafka command reports the committed offset (CURRENT-OFFSET), the newest offset (LOG-END-OFFSET), and the gap between them (LAG). During the promotion, lag was in single digits on every partition, while the database query showed hundreds of thousands of pending tasks. Together, the two results placed the problem in the sender stage.

Timestamps recorded at each stage, from the order commit to provider acceptance, show where the time was spent, provided each timestamp has a documented meaning. “Published,” for instance, could mean when the relay sent the event or when Kafka stored it. Clocks on separate machines also drift slightly apart, so an interval calculated from two machines’ timestamps can come out negative. A negative interval points to clock skew or a timestamp defect, and it should be investigated rather than rounded to zero.

Capacity Scaling

Once task creation had been ruled out, the engineers looked at sender throughput, the provider’s rate limits, and the database work involved in claiming and completing tasks. Added capacity helps only at the stage where work accumulates, and even there it has limits. More consumer processes help when processing is CPU-bound and some partitions are unassigned, but they make a database bottleneck worse by adding concurrent writes, and they cannot speed up a single busy key. More senders help only up to the provider’s rate allowance; beyond it, they turn a backlog into rejected requests and more retries. For that reason, Baodium tested higher sender throughput against the provider’s limits before relying on it during an incident.

When capacity cannot be raised, the product needs a planned response. Optional marketing emails can wait, but accepted order confirmations must be sent or explicitly marked as failed. Deleting them to improve the backlog numbers breaks a promise made to customers.

Consumer Rebalancing

Scaling and deployments change the membership of a consumer group, and every such change triggers a rebalance, in which Kafka reassigns partitions among the group’s members. A deployment, a crashed consumer, or a consumer that misses its five-minute polling deadline all cause one.

A rebalance resembles a shift change on a production line, where a station passes to a new worker while the previous worker may be holding a half-finished item. Suppose consumer A is processing offset 500 in partition 3. It creates the email task, but before it commits, a rebalance assigns partition 3 to consumer B. Consumer A’s commit is rejected because it no longer owns the partition, and consumer B starts from the last committed offset, which is 500. The same event is processed twice.

A rebalance is therefore another source of redelivery, and the protections we already have handle it: the claims table, the business constraint, and idempotency keys on calls to the provider. This is one reason to build idempotency into every consumer from the start, rather than adding it for particular failure cases.

Some records take longer to process than the polling deadline allows. For those, the consumer hands records to a separate pool of workers and continues polling Kafka in the meantime, so that it is not assumed to have failed. When a partition is taken away, the consumer stops starting new work for it, lets work already in progress finish or cancels it, and commits only offsets whose work is complete.

Two settings from Listing \(\ref{lst:ch12-consumer}\) reduce the disruption. The cooperative sticky assignor reassigns only the partitions that need to change, instead of taking every partition from every consumer and redistributing them all, so most consumers keep working through the change. A fixed group.instance.id lets a consumer that restarts within its session timeout reclaim its own partitions without any rebalance, so a rolling deployment does not reshuffle the group.

Failure Handling

So far we have assumed that every event can eventually be processed. In practice, some cannot. Failures fall into two classes, depending on whether a later retry can succeed:

Transient failures,

such as a brief database outage, resolve on their own. The consumer retries a limited number of times with increasing delays.

Permanent failures,

such as a malformed event or an unsupported schema version, fail on every attempt. Retrying them wastes capacity and blocks the records behind them in the partition.

A permanently failing record has to be preserved, together with the reason it failed, so that someone can repair it. Records that cannot even be decoded need particular care, because they fail before the application’s normal handler runs. A consumer that reads the raw bytes first can save the original payload along with its topic, partition, and offset.

Dead-Letter Topics

Post offices have long kept a dead-letter office, where mail that cannot be delivered is held until someone works out where it belongs. A dead-letter topic serves the same purpose for records that fail permanently. The consumer copies the failed record there and continues with the next one, so a single malformed event does not halt an entire partition.

Sending a record to the dead-letter topic does not complete its work, since the customer has not yet received an email. It records that the work is unfinished and hands it to someone who can fix it. For that reason, every dead-letter topic needs an owner and its own measurements, such as the number of records waiting and the age of the oldest one.

Ordering After Failure

Setting a record aside can break ordering. Suppose an OrderConfirmed event fails permanently, the consumer sets it aside, and the next event for the same order is OrderShipped. The consumer now has a shipped order that was never confirmed. It has three options, each with a cost:

  1. Halt the whole partition until the failed record is repaired. Ordering is preserved, but every order in the partition waits.

  2. Hold back only that order’s events while processing other orders. The hold must be stored durably, because an in-memory flag is lost on restart.

  3. Use a handler that can reconstruct the missing state, for example by asking Order Service for the order’s current status.

Whichever option the team chooses, the repair procedure names an owner and defines how a corrected event is put back into the stream.

Replay and Schema Evolution

Because Kafka retains events, a consumer can reset its bookmark to an earlier offset and process old events again. This is called replay, and whether it is safe depends on what the consumer does with each event.

Replaying events into a Catalog copy is safe and often useful: the engineers replay into a fresh destination, compare it with the current copy, and switch readers once the rebuilt copy has been verified. Replaying events into Notification Service is another matter, because its effect is to send email. Without the claims table, a replay of 10,000 order events sends 10,000 confirmation emails for orders placed weeks ago.

Before any replay, the team therefore decides what the replay is allowed to cause. When customers need a replacement email, for instance because the original used the wrong template, Baodium creates new repair tasks for exactly those customers rather than rewinding a consumer and letting old events run through it again.

Schema Evolution

Replay has a second consequence: a consumer may read events that were written months ago in an older format. It must therefore understand every schema version that remains in the topic, not only the current one.

Adding an optional field is safe for new events, but a consumer reading an old event finds the field missing and needs a rule for what that means. If discount_applied is missing, it might mean that no discount was applied, or that the producer did not record discounts when the event was written. The event contract must define which interpretation applies to the missing field in each retained schema version.

Changes in meaning are more dangerous than changes in structure. If a field changes from a gross amount to a net amount, its type is unchanged and validation passes, yet every report built on it becomes wrong without any error. A change in meaning therefore requires a new field or a new event version. Consumer tests include sample events from every retained version, because tests against current events cannot catch problems with older ones.

Stateful Stream Processing

Every consumer we have discussed handles each event independently. Some work, however, needs many events together. Baodium’s merchant sales report publishes each merchant’s order total for every five-minute interval: the processor reads order events, adds each order to a running total for its merchant and interval, and publishes the totals.

The running total is state, and state introduces a failure mode that independent processing does not have. Suppose the processor adds a $120 order to a merchant’s total and crashes before committing its bookmark. After the restart, it reads the same order again and adds another $120, so the report overstates the merchant’s sales, and no error is raised. To prevent this, the processor has to save its state and its bookmark together, in one atomic step.

Stream-processing frameworks such as Kafka Streams and Apache Flink provide that step. They keep state locally, back it up continuously, and take periodic checkpoints that capture the state and the bookmark at the same moment. After a crash, they restore both from the same checkpoint, so each event is reflected in the state exactly once. Restoring a large state can take several minutes, during which no new events are processed, so the engineers measure restore time with production-sized data.

Event Time and Watermarks

The report also has to decide which clock assigns an order to an interval. Processing time is when the processor handles the event, and event time is when the order was placed. An order placed at 10:00 but delayed in transit until 10:36 belongs in the 10:00 interval, so the report uses event time.

Event time raises a practical difficulty. The processor has to decide when the 10:00–10:05 interval is complete and its total can be published, yet a delayed event for that interval can arrive at any time.

A watermark is the processor’s estimate that no more events from before a given time will arrive. It works like a teacher collecting exams, who decides how long to wait for latecomers before starting to mark. When the watermark passes the end of an interval, the processor publishes that interval’s total.

Because a watermark is an estimate, some events arrive after it. The report’s contract defines what happens to these late events: they may revise the earlier total, produce a separate correction, or go to a repair queue. Consumers of the report also need to know which behavior to expect, because a consumer that adds each revised total to the previous one, instead of replacing it, counts the same orders twice.

Failure Testing

Each mechanism in this chapter exists to handle an interruption between two durable steps, so the most useful tests create exactly those interruptions. Baodium’s test suite includes the following cases:

  • A consumer is stopped after creating a task but before committing its bookmark. The redelivered event must not create a second task.

  • A sender is stopped after the provider accepts an email. The task must become UNCERTAIN and be resolved through the provider’s status lookup.

  • Malformed events, unsupported versions, and events that violate business rules pass through the consumer. Each must reach the dead-letter topic with its original payload intact.

  • A rebalance occurs while workers are partway through records.

  • A replay includes old schema versions and events whose claims are near the end of their retention.

  • Recovery is tested while new events continue to arrive, not only against a fixed backlog.

Each test is judged by the final outcome rather than by Kafka metrics. Every accepted task must end up sent, durably pending, or explicitly failed, and a drop in consumer lag proves nothing if the work has accumulated somewhere else.

Summary

Moving notifications and projections out of a synchronous request allowed Baodium to complete its own transaction before those consumers finished. It also created independent work that needed durable publication, defined completion states, and recovery ownership. The transactional outbox recorded the business change and the obligation to publish within one transaction; the relay and consumer then had to preserve the required per-order order and tolerate repeated delivery.

Partitions made concurrent processing possible, while operation identities and database constraints prevented duplicate consumption from producing duplicate local effects. Calls to external providers required an additional state because a consumer could lose the response after the provider had completed the action. Dead-letter handling kept persistent failures available for investigation, and stream-processing watermarks established how long late input could change a time-based result.

During the promotion incident, the useful measurement was the arrival and completion rate at each stage. A growing queue alone did not identify the bottleneck; the team had to find the stage whose completion rate was below incoming demand and establish how much spare throughput recovery would require. Chapter 13 applies this resource and outcome accounting to model-based features, where request success can remain high while recommendation quality deteriorates.
